faqs.question: What is a good witch pun?
faqs.answer: A good witch pun swaps one witchy word into a phrase people already know, such as "the flight went off without a witch" or "broom and gloom". The best ones change a single sound, so the listener gets both meanings in under a second.

faqs.question: What are some short witch puns for Instagram?
faqs.answer: Spelling-swap lines read fastest in a caption because the eye catches the twist: "witchful thinking", "midnight snacks from the coven-ience store" or "a full brew-ha-ha". Every line in this post runs between 40 and 83 characters, so each fits a phone screen in one or two lines.

faqs.question: Why do witch and which sound the same?
faqs.answer: They sound the same only for speakers with the wine–whine merger, where the old breathy wh sound has dropped out. Speakers who keep the older distinction say "which" with a breathy /ʍ/ sound, so witch/which puns land better for them in writing than aloud.

faqs.question: Where does the word hex come from?
faqs.answer: Hex was first attested in English around 1830, borrowed from Pennsylvania Dutch hexe, "to practise witchcraft", from German Hexe, "witch". The hex in hexagon and hexadecimal is unrelated, which is why hex puns can go magical or nerdy.

faqs.question: Are coven and convent the same word?
faqs.answer: They are doublets: both come from Latin conventum, "a gathering", from convenire, "to come together". Coven also contains "oven", which is where most coven puns get their kitchen jokes.

faqs.question: Why do people groan at puns?
faqs.answer: A 2023 Journal of Neuroscience fMRI study of 26 adults found that getting a joke and enjoying it use partly different brain systems. A groan usually means the listener understood the double meaning instantly but chose not to reward it with a laugh.

faqs.question: Are these witch puns clean enough for kids?
faqs.answer: Yes, none of the 49 lines uses innuendo, insults or anything gory. The hex and curse lines suit older kids better, since very young children may take a pretend curse literally.

faqs.question: Is it rude to make witch puns around someone who practises Wicca?
faqs.answer: Light puns about brooms, cauldrons and potions rarely offend, but jokes about cursing people can feel like mockery of a real faith. If you know the person practises, ask first or stick to the broom and brew groups.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a witch pun and a witch pickup line?
faqs.answer: A pun is a joke built on one word with two meanings, told to anyone. A pickup line is aimed at a specific person to start a conversation, and may or may not use wordplay at all.

faqs.question: When is Halloween in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is 31 October every year: Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027. All Saints' Day follows on 1 November.

faqs.question: Can I send one witch pun to one person as a Halloween page?
faqs.answer: Yes. The regular SubhSandesh Halloween card takes about five minutes and holds up to six photos and a letter, while the premium page adds a voice note of up to 60 seconds so you can say the pun yourself.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Witch Puns: 49 Original Lines Sorted by the Word Doing the Trick

The best witch puns hang on one word with two jobs: witch and which, a spell you cast and a word you spell, a broom you sweep with and a broom you fly. Below are 49 original, clean witch puns sorted by that source word, so you choose by mechanism rather than scrolling. Across the 5,199 personalised pages built on SubhSandesh since March 2026, 48.3% of views came from a phone, so every line here fits one glance on a small screen.

A shared page also averages 11.1 views, so a line is likely to be seen more than once. Two studies on why puns land, a table on which family suits Instagram or a party, and the cases to avoid follow the lists.

## What makes a witch pun work?

A pun is a joke in which one sound or spelling carries two meanings, and the listener has to hold both for a moment. Witch puns are unusually rich because the seven core words used below have tangled histories.

[Wiktionary's entry for "witch"](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/witch) lists "which" as a homophone only for speakers with the wine–whine merger. Speakers who keep the old distinction say "which" with a breathy /ʍ/, so for them the joke is weaker aloud. The word itself runs back to Old English *wiċċe*, a female witch, and *wiċċa*, a male one.

"Spell" meaning a charm comes from Old English *spell*, "news, story", while "a spell" of cold weather comes from a separate verb meaning to stand in for someone. One witch line can therefore carry three senses at once.

## 49 witch puns grouped by the word doing the work

Each group opens with the fact behind its puns, then seven lines. Pick the word that suits your costume.

### 1. Witch and which: homophone puns

These swap "witch" in for "which", "rich", "hitch" or "wish". On screen the spelling shows the twist, so they read better in text than aloud.

- The flight to the coven went off without a witch.
- Her birthday witch list has one item: a faster broom.
- Sweeping the whole house in one night is witchful thinking.
- Her fortune teller says she'll end up witch beyond her wildest dreams.
- Pick witchever potion you like; they all taste faintly of pond.
- Three hundred years with the same broom, and not one seven-year witch.
- She traded the old broom for a new model; the old one called it a bait and s-witch.

### 2. Spell puns: one word, three meanings

The verb "to spell" letters grew from the same Germanic root as the magic noun. The weather sense is a different word that merged in spelling, so these lines can stack meanings.

- Cold spell this week? She swears she only cast a mild one.
- The rumour that she can't cook was quickly dispelled.
- She took a long spell off witching to raise a family of crows.
- She's on a hot spell: three charms, zero misfires.
- Her apprentice can't spell "abracadabra" the same way twice.
- Read the room before you read the spell.
- The library charges late fees on spellbooks in newts.

### 3. Broom puns

"Broom" comes from Old English *brōm*, the shrub whose twigs made the first brooms. It rhymes with room, groom, gloom and bloom, which is most of the joke supply.

- Weather forecast for the coven: broom and gloom.
- Make broom on the porch; six witches are landing at once.
- The bride wore black and the broom wore a bow tie.
- She learned to fly late in life; a true late broomer.
- From up there she gets a sweeping view of the whole town.
- She only flies manual; she calls it a broomstick shift.
- Before the big flight she brushed up on her landings.

### 4. Brew puns

"Brew" swaps neatly into rude, brute, rumour and the old word brouhaha. Most of these change one sound in a well-worn phrase.

- The potion contest ended in a full brew-ha-ha.
- One sip of the morning potion and she had a brewed awakening.
- The stuck jar finally opened by brewed force.
- There's a brewmour going round that she dyes her cat.
- She gives brewtal honesty about everyone's potions.
- Sunday brew-nch with the coven starts at midnight sharp.
- Ask her what's brewing and she'll say "Thursday".

### 5. Cauldron puns

"Cauldron" came into English from Norman French *caudron*, from Latin *caldus*, "hot"; the *l* was added later to look Latin. Its cousins are caldera and chowder.

- Coven dinners are always pot luck; the cauldron decides who eats.
- Three hours stirring and she went completely stir-crazy.
- She's in hot water again, but she's the one who lit the fire.
- The cauldron called the kettle black and nobody was surprised.
- When the coven argues, the cauldron tells everyone to simmer down.
- In Scots, "cauld" means cold, so a pot left out overnight is a true cauld-ron.
- She cooks chowder in the cauldron, so it's basically a family reunion.

### 6. Hex puns

[Wiktionary's "hex" entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hex) dates the word to about 1830, borrowed from Pennsylvania Dutch *hexe*, "to practise witchcraft", from German *Hexe*, "witch". The unrelated "hex" short for hexadecimal or hexagon gives a second, nerdier set.

- Her favourite shape is a hexagon: six sides, every one cursed.
- Of course her wifi password is in hexadecimal.
- Her morning routine is ten minutes of hexercise.
- She charges hextra for curses booked on a Sunday.
- The results of the love potion were completely unhexpected.
- Her spellbook left the new apprentice thoroughly per-hexed.
- She signs every curse "best hexes", never "best wishes".

### 7. Coven puns

[Wiktionary's "coven" entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/coven) traces the word to Latin *conventum*, "a gathering", and lists convent as its doublet. Coven also hides "oven", which every gingerbread-house fan noticed long ago.

- She opened a bakery called The Coven; everything comes out of the oven.
- Kitchen rule: what happens in the oven stays in the coven.
- Midnight snacks come from the 24-hour coven-ience store.
- Her coven keeps strictly uncoventional hours.
- She's a coven-tional witch: pointy hat, black cat, no surprises.
- The coven signed a coven-ant: nobody borrows a broom without asking.
- The coven and the convent are cousins who stopped speaking.

## Why do puns land? What two studies found

Puns work because the brain briefly keeps both meanings switched on. In a [2015 PLOS ONE study by Rose, Spalek and Abdel Rahman](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4482729), 88 native German speakers heard puns or ordinary jokes, then named pictures of objects with double-meaning names such as *Schloss*, lock and castle. Only after puns did words tied to the hidden second meaning speed up naming, a sign the other sense stayed active.

Getting a joke and enjoying it are separate steps. A [2023 Journal of Neuroscience fMRI study by Prenger and colleagues](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10711695) scanned 26 young adults and found that comprehension engaged both the dorsal and ventral striatum, while appreciation engaged only the ventral striatum, a region tied to reward.

That split explains the groan. A witch pun is understood almost instantly, but enjoyment depends on whether the listener likes being caught by two meanings at once, so a groan often means the first half worked.

## Which witch pun works where, including Instagram

Here the seven families fall into three mechanisms. The table shows how each fares aloud and the median character length of this post's lines.

| Pun family | Mechanism | Said aloud | Median length (this list) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Witch/which, coven | Spelling swap seen on screen | Weaker; needs the spelling | 61 characters |
| Spell, broom | Real double meaning or rhyme | Works aloud and in text | 53 characters |
| Brew, hex, cauldron | Idiom with one sound changed | Works aloud for most listeners | 56 characters |

For an Instagram caption, the spelling-swap families win because the eye catches "witchful" or "coven-ience" before the brain decides to scroll. All 49 lines run between 40 and 83 characters, short enough to sit on one or two lines of a phone screen.

Spoken at a party, the idiom groups travel best. "Brewed awakening" works whether or not your listener merges *wh* and *w*, while "without a witch" can fall flat with someone who says "which" with a breathy /ʍ/.

## Turn one witch pun into a Halloween page for one person

Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027 are the dates to aim for. A pun on paper gets read once; a shared SubhSandesh page collects 11.1 views on average, so the line keeps working.

For a quick, playful line, the [interactive Halloween card where they carve a pumpkin](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about five minutes: six photos at most, your word glowing in the jack-o'-lantern, and a letter read by flashlight. That letter is where a broom or brew pun sits best.

For a bigger moment, the [premium Halloween page with your own voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about ten minutes and lets you say the pun yourself in a recording of 60 seconds or less, with 12 photos, a timed unlock and one reply back. Platform-wide, 38.5% of creators password-protect their page, an option both templates give you.

Punning at someone who hates Halloween? [Pick a non-spooky SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) instead and keep the witch line for next October.

## When should you not use a witch pun?

Puns aimed at a real woman can read as name-calling. Lines that use "witch" as a stand-in for a ruder word land as an insult, which is why none of the 49 above calls a real person a witch.

Some friends practise Wicca or modern witchcraft as a faith. A cauldron joke is usually fine, but a cursing pun can feel like mockery, so ask first or stick to brooms.

For a crowd, skip the page entirely. Each Halloween template greets exactly one person and cannot invite a party, so a pun meant for a room of 30 belongs on a sign by the snack table.

## Sources

- Wiktionary contributors. ["witch"](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/witch). *Wiktionary* (continuously edited, no publication date).
- Wiktionary contributors. ["coven"](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/coven). *Wiktionary* (continuously edited, no publication date).
- Wiktionary contributors. ["hex"](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hex). *Wiktionary* (continuously edited, no publication date).
- Rose, S. B., Spalek, K. and Abdel Rahman, R. (26 June 2015). [Listening to Puns Elicits the Co-Activation of Alternative Homophone Meanings during Language Production](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4482729). *PLOS ONE* 10(6): e0130853.
- Prenger, M. et al. (6 December 2023). [Establishing the Roles of the Dorsal and Ventral Striatum in Humor Comprehension and Appreciation with fMRI](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10711695). *Journal of Neuroscience*.
